posts.note: Republication (2024-06-22) of two 2022 essays on the Medical Loss Ratio with a short 2024 preamble and postscript. Forward-looking content is structural (costs, premiums, payer behavior) rather than dated events.
Republication (2024-06-24) of a July 10, 2023 essay on PBMs with a 2024 preamble. Two logged quotes are third-party forecasts (Lina Khan, CVS CEO Merlo) with own_claim false.

statements.quote: Sadly, people waiting on transcranial magnetic stimulation or esketamine will still be waiting for prior authorization for several more weeks.
statements.context: Republished 2022 essay on the Medical Loss Ratio (MLR). Caption-style aside after the Harrowing of Hell image: patients seeking TMS or esketamine will keep waiting on payer prior authorization for weeks. Generic claim about ongoing payer practice, not a specific event.
statements.note: Glib aside; continuation claim about prior authorization delays. Body text written in 2022, post dated 2024-06-22.

statements.quote: But overall, any contention that reducing cost is what will happen is fictional at best and fraudulent at worst.
statements.context: Section 'Let's Play Pretend!'. The author lists major carriers (Blue Cross, United, Cigna, Aetna, Anthem, Magellan, Oscar, Elevance, Evernorth) that claim to control costs. He denies that cost reduction will happen under the MLR incentive structure.
statements.confidence_phrase: fictional at best and fraudulent at worst
statements.note: Negative call: insurers will not reduce total healthcare cost.

statements.quote: With incentives for costs to go up, it will happen!
statements.context: Closing line of the MLR mechanics section, right after noting that Amazon bought One Medical. The author asserts that because the MLR rewards higher spend, healthcare costs will rise.
statements.note: Core thesis: MLR incentives push total healthcare cost up.

statements.quote: Costs have to go up every year, and because multiple companies are in the space, they essentially have to go up somewhat uniformly across all companies. That way, premiums for everybody go up by some semi-palatable amount yearly.
statements.context: MLR mechanics section. The author predicts that health insurer costs and premiums rise every year, roughly uniformly across carriers, as a structural consequence of the 80/20 MLR rule.
statements.note: Compound recurring claim: costs rise yearly, uniformly across carriers, premiums rise yearly.

statements.quote: It can tilt backward and forwards between Harvard, Princeton, and Yale, but no one has to worry that UMass will knock them out of the running for the top three spots.
statements.context: MLR mechanics section, comparing health plan comparison shopping to college rankings. Metaphor: the ranking among the top carriers may shuffle, but no outsider will displace the top health plans.
statements.note: Metaphor for payer market concentration staying stable; underlying claim reads as sincere. Borderline.

statements.quote: The incentives driving the balance sheets of our major payers force them inevitably to higher costs, sickness, and premiums. Rinse, repeat, every year, without end, until we are all broke and dead.
statements.context: MLR mechanics section, right after 'I do not believe there is a sinister plot.' The author predicts that major payers are driven inevitably to higher costs, more sickness and higher premiums, repeating every year without end.
statements.note: Compound claim: higher costs, sickness and premiums. Hyperbolic ending ('until we are all broke and dead').

statements.quote: Expecting them to lower costs, in violation of their fiduciary role to shareholders, however, is a fever dream.
statements.context: Second half (mental health system section). The author says payers generate shareholder value and will not lower costs because that would violate their fiduciary duty to shareholders.
statements.note: Negative call; restates the earlier claim that payers will not reduce cost.

statements.quote: My Spirited Dissent…Won’t Matter.
statements.context: Section heading before the argument that insisting on non-scientific standards of proof is inhumane and that payer coverage of more remission-inducing treatments would mean less illness but less profit. The author expects his own dissent to have no effect on payer behavior.
statements.note: Section heading; call about the author's own influence. The 2024 preamble later claims the articles did influence OCD coverage policy.

statements.quote: If we had more treatments that lead to remission paid for by payers, it would mean less depression, PTSD , OCD, and more. But... Less profits.
statements.context: Section 'My Spirited Dissent...Won't Matter.' Conditional: if payers covered more remission-inducing treatments, population depression, PTSD and OCD would fall, and payer profits would fall.
statements.note: Conditional counterfactual; compound (less illness, less profit).

statements.quote: Claims are going to be administered. Claims are going to be denied. Prior authorization is going to be required. The machinery of prior authorization will be tinkered with.
statements.context: Section 'The Fall', describing healthcare megacorps (Optum, UnitedHealth) with no sinister plot. The author predicts that claims denial and prior authorization will continue and the prior authorization machinery will keep being adjusted.
statements.confidence_phrase: are going to be; will be
statements.note: Continuation claim about payer practice.

statements.quote: And if we find evidence of illegal practices, we will not hesitate to act.
statements.context: 2024 preamble. The author quotes FTC Chair Lina Khan on the FTC PBM inquiry: PBMs have not fully complied with FTC orders, the FTC will use its legal authorities to compel compliance and will act if it finds illegal practices. The author cites it as evidence the PBM issue has come to a head.
statements.note: Quoted third party (Lina Khan, FTC). The author cites it approvingly but does not restate it as his own call.

statements.quote: More is coming on that stupid saga
statements.context: Aside about legal threat letters the author received from a Troutman Pepper partner after he complained about his own health plan's drug coverage. He promises future newsletter coverage of the dispute.
statements.note: Call about the author's own newsletter content; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: expect more of it in the years to come and are confident that we ourselves are key disruptors
statements.context: Bullet quoting CVS CEO Larry Merlo on competition among PBMs ('We welcome competition'). The author presents it as an example of industry doublespeak, not as his own expectation.
statements.note: Quoted third party (CVS CEO Merlo); the author cites it as doublespeak and does not adopt it.

statements.quote: If one were paying for interplanetary travel, the trip from Earth to Saturn, at $1 a meter, would be affordable next year if costs go up at current rates — it’s 1.38 trillion meters away.
statements.context: Section 'Intergalactic Expense is Not Enough', after citing 2022 Big Insurance revenue of $1.25 trillion and profits of $69.3 billion. Implied numeric call: at current growth rates, Big Health revenue exceeds $1.38 trillion next year. Original text written July 2023, republished June 2024.
statements.note: Humorous framing (author calls it an exaggeration), but the arithmetic extrapolation (revenue above $1.38T next year) reads as a real expectation.

statements.quote: We’re always moving in the direction of value. We can never get there. This “never” is important to understand; just like the mob, Big Health really can not stop putting the squeeze on you.
statements.context: Section on 'value' rhetoric in Big Health podcasts. The author asserts Big Health (insurer-owned PBMs) will never reach 'value' and can never stop raising costs on members, because doing so would violate fiduciary duty to shareholders.
statements.note: Negative call; same structural thesis as the MLR post.

statements.quote: The Culture of Obedience, endless doublespeak, complexity, and mind-numbing profits can’t be undone by outsiders. It’s too powerful.
statements.context: Section comparing the RICO takedown of the Mafia to Big Health. The author claims outsiders (regulators, critics) cannot dismantle the Big Health and PBM system; insiders are needed.
statements.note: Negative call; followed by the normative 'We need heroes from inside that culture to tear it apart'.

statements.quote: The Big Health Mafia used complexity to shake us down. In turn, it will be taken down by those who ran the scam.
statements.context: Section 'The Empire Strikes Back'. The author predicts that Big Health (insurer-owned PBMs) will be taken down by former insiders speaking out, citing Wendell Potter, Dave Chase and Mark Cuban, and the Consolidated Appropriations Act 2021 fiduciary rule.
statements.note: Direct call; mechanism is former insiders plus CAA fiduciary duty litigation.

statements.quote: Mobsters eventually turned into rats for less. Are the contract killers working at PBMs less tough than Junior Soprano? I can’t wait to find out.
statements.context: Section 'Big Healthcare, Meet The Enforcers', after quoting the Department of Labor on criminal ERISA penalties of up to ten years. The author implies PBM insiders will turn informant under ERISA and CAA criminal exposure, as mobsters did under RICO.
statements.note: Implicit expectation phrased as a question; borderline.

statements.quote: Meanwhile, that cost-plus pharmacy card will work at most pharmacies.
statements.context: Closing section. The author asserts the Rethinking Heroes / CapitalRx cost-plus discount card will work at most US pharmacies. Footnote 23 says he built the first version in 2021 and works with founder Jerry Ashton.
statements.note: Author's own project; CONTROL candidate. Product functionality claim more than an event forecast.

statements.quote: They failed, but others will sue and win. It’s already heating up with Perez, Ca 2021 enforcement and regulatory scrutiny.
statements.context: Footnote 9, on the law firm's late legal reply to the author's ADA complaint against his health plan. The author predicts other plaintiffs will sue Big Health plans and PBMs for fiduciary breach under ERISA and CAA 2021 and win.
statements.note: Footnote; litigation outcome call.

statements.quote: I imagine the discovery, in that case, is most of the evidence needed for this one, vastly reducing the cost of the litigation…
statements.context: Footnote 12 on Ford's Sherman Act antitrust suit against the Blue Cross plans. The author expects discovery from the prior $2.7b class action settlement to supply most of the evidence for Ford's case and greatly reduce its litigation cost.
statements.note: Footnote; hedged call about the course of a specific lawsuit.

statements.quote: Finally, I will explain the legal strategy I see starting to solve this problem.
statements.context: Roadmap paragraph at the start of the 2023 essay. The author says the legal strategy (CAA 2021 fiduciary duty and ERISA liability for employers) is starting to solve the PBM problem.
statements.note: Mostly an article roadmap; weak predictive content that the legal strategy is beginning to work. Borderline.
